title: Write, Execute, Refine: From Skill Followers to Skill Optimizers via Reinforcement Learning from Execution Feedback

visual_explainer.blocker: Two isolated paper-specific GPT Image attempts in this run (CABLE and ArborMem) both ignored their grounded single-paper briefs and rendered a generic Agent Memory Radar dashboard with fabricated paper metadata. Visual QA rejected both; further required-paper retries were stopped to avoid publishing ungrounded visuals until the paper-identity failure is resolved.

analysis.tldr: WER learns a persistent skill-writer policy from execution consequences rather than treating skill refinement as prompt-only reflection: candidate skill documents are executed by a frozen agent, scored by programmatic verifiers, and used for group-relative RL, while mixed success/failure trajectories bootstrap the next refinement state.
analysis.problem: Static skills and reflection-based rewriting receive weak supervision about whether a procedural edit actually improves tool execution. A skill can sound better yet make the frozen executor worse, and repeated refinement can overfit or drift without consequence-grounded training.
analysis.core_idea: Place a trainable Skill Optimizer outside a frozen executor. Given the current skill, task context, history, and execution evidence, sample candidate skill documents; execute each multiple times with the same frozen agent/tool environment; score outcomes with programmatic verifiers; update the optimizer with group-relative RL. For multi-stage refinement, retain mixed-outcome cases so successful and failed executions of the same skill/task become the next phase's diagnostic state.

memory_design.write: The optimizer writes/refines natural-language skill artifacts; candidate skills are versioned through iterative training phases.
memory_design.organize: Persistent procedural state is the skill document plus execution histories used to condition later refinements.
memory_design.read: A frozen downstream agent consumes the current skill during tool execution; the optimizer consumes matched execution evidence when producing the next skill.
memory_design.update_forget: Execution-scored RL updates the skill-writer policy and repeated refinement updates the artifact; deeper refinement is stopped when gains saturate, but long-term skill deletion/governance is not studied.

compared_to: No Skill and the seed skill under the same frozen executor
An untrained Qwen3-4B optimizer under the same refinement workflow
General-purpose optimizer models including GPT-5.5 under the same workflow
analysis.evidence: On BFCL v4, No Skill scores 68.83, the seed skill 67.28, the untrained Qwen3-4B optimizer 67.28, and WER-trained 4B reaches 76.63: +9.35 over the same untrained optimizer. On tau2, untrained is 40.43 and WER is 50.72 (+10.29). BFCL checkpoints rise 69.35→71.29→76.63 across phases; an extra refinement step falls to 75.33, so more editing is not monotonically beneficial. The trained 4B optimizer also exceeds GPT-5.5's 74.75 in the reported same-workflow BFCL comparison.
analysis.why_it_matters: WER moves procedural-memory evolution from 'rewrite a skill' to 'learn the writer from the downstream consequences of its own revisions.' That makes execution feedback a training signal for the state-transition policy itself rather than only a post-hoc evaluator.
limitations: Training is rollout- and verifier-intensive and assumes programmatic success signals in stateful tool environments.
The final protocol uses a stronger model to merge domain skills, so the end package is not produced solely by the learned 4B optimizer.
Evaluation covers two tool-agent benchmark families rather than long-running deployment or open-ended skill libraries.
Repeated refinement saturates and can regress, so an online stopping/governance policy remains necessary.
